concepts.name: Radiopharmaceutical
concepts.statement: A radiopharmaceutical is a compound tagged with a radioactive nuclide and chosen because the body sends it to the organ under study. Because $\gamma$ rays pass easily out of the body and a nucleus radiates the same whatever compound it sits in, detectors outside the body can see where the compound has gone.

concepts.name: Technetium-99m
concepts.statement: One nuclide carries perhaps 80 percent of all nuclear medicine, and the reasons are the chapter's physics in miniature: a single clean $\gamma$ energy, a short half-life that limits the dose, and a parent that decays into it on site.

concepts.name: Anger camera
concepts.statement: The Anger camera images a radiopharmaceutical with a lead collimator that passes only $\gamma$ rays traveling along its holes, a scintillator that turns each $\gamma$ ray into light, and photomultipliers that turn the light into a signal. The image it forms is flat and carries no depth.

concepts.name: SPECT
concepts.statement: Single-photon-emission computed tomography images a $\gamma$-emitting radiopharmaceutical. It surrounds the patient with detectors and combines their images by computer into a three-dimensional picture, as x-ray CT does for shadows. It gains depth at the cost of resolution.

concepts.name: PET
concepts.statement: PET is the cleanest use of conservation laws in medicine: an annihilating positron and electron at rest must send two equal 0.511-MeV $\gamma$ rays in opposite directions, so two detectors firing together name the line the source lies on.

concepts.name: Finding a mass from activity
concepts.statement: The mass of a radioactive sample follows from its activity and half-life: the activity and half-life give the number of nuclei, and Avogadro's number and the molar mass turn that number into a mass. Medical activities of a few millicuries correspond to astonishingly small masses.

concepts.name: Tagged compound
concepts.statement: A compound is tagged when a radioactive nuclide is attached to it, so that the nuclide's radiation shows where the compound goes.

concepts.name: Radiation damage to DNA
concepts.statement: Every biological effect of radiation, from cancer to its cure, follows from this one statement. It explains why rapidly reproducing cells, including cancer cells, are the most sensitive.

concepts.name: Radiation dose
concepts.statement: The absorbed dose is the ionizing energy deposited per kilogram of the tissue affected. It is measured in rad, where $1\;\text{rad} = 0.01\;\text{J/kg}$, or in gray, where $1\;\text{Gy} = 1\;\text{J/kg} = 100\;\text{rad}$.

concepts.name: Relative biological effectiveness
concepts.statement: The relative biological effectiveness (RBE), or quality factor, of a type of radiation is the factor by which its biological effect per unit of absorbed dose exceeds that of x rays. Short-range radiation such as $\alpha$ particles concentrates its damage, which is harder to repair, and so has a large RBE.

concepts.name: Dose equivalent
concepts.statement: The dose equivalent is the absorbed dose multiplied by the RBE, a number proportional to the biological effect: $\text{rem} = \text{rad}\times\text{RBE}$ and $\text{Sv} = \text{Gy}\times\text{RBE}$. Dose limits and risks are stated in this quantity.

concepts.name: Calculating a dose
concepts.statement: The dose from a source is found by following its decays into joules per kilogram: the activity and time give the number of decays, the energy per decay gives the energy deposited, the mass of tissue gives the dose in grays, and the RBE gives the dose in sieverts. Activity is not to be confused with dose along the way.

concepts.name: Immediate effects of a dose
concepts.statement: A single whole-body dose below about 0.1 Sv has no observable immediate effect, a dose near 1 Sv causes radiation sickness, and a dose near 5 Sv is fatal to about half of those who receive it. Blood counts fall first because blood cells reproduce fastest.

concepts.name: Linear hypothesis
concepts.statement: The linear hypothesis assumes that the risk of a radiation-induced cancer is proportional to the dose, even at doses too low for any effect to be observed. Scaling down from high doses in this way gives about $10/10^{6}\;\text{rem}\cdot\text{y}$ for the risk of cancer.

concepts.name: Background radiation
concepts.statement: Everyone receives background radiation, about 3 mSv a year on average, from cosmic rays, from rocks and soil, from the body's own nuclides and, above all, from radon. Its size varies from place to place and is the natural yardstick for every other dose.

concepts.name: Radiation protection
concepts.statement: A dose is limited in only three ways: by keeping the time of exposure short, by increasing the distance from the source and by placing shielding between the source and the body.

concepts.name: Rad
concepts.statement: The rad, short for radiation absorbed dose, is the dose that deposits 0.01 J of ionizing energy in each kilogram of tissue.

concepts.name: Gray
concepts.statement: The gray is the SI unit of absorbed dose, the dose that deposits 1 J of ionizing energy in each kilogram of tissue; one gray is 100 rad.

concepts.name: Rem
concepts.statement: The rem, short for roentgen equivalent man, is the unit of dose equivalent that goes with the rad: a dose in rad times the RBE of the radiation gives the dose equivalent in rem.

concepts.name: Sievert
concepts.statement: The sievert is the SI unit of dose equivalent: a dose in grays times the RBE of the radiation gives the dose equivalent in sieverts, and one sievert is 100 rem.

concepts.name: Low dose
concepts.statement: A low dose is a dose of less than about 0.1 Sv (10 rem), below which no immediate effect can be observed.

concepts.name: Moderate dose
concepts.statement: A moderate dose is a dose from about 0.1 Sv to 1 Sv (10 to 100 rem), which can cause measurable changes in the blood and, near the top of the range, radiation sickness.

concepts.name: High dose
concepts.statement: A high dose is a dose greater than about 1 Sv (100 rem), which causes radiation sickness and, at several sieverts, can be fatal.

concepts.name: Hormesis
concepts.statement: Hormesis is the proposal that a very low dose of radiation may be beneficial, stimulating the body's repair mechanisms; the evidence for it is not conclusive.

concepts.name: Shielding
concepts.statement: Shielding is a layer of material placed between a radiation source and the body to absorb the radiation and so reduce the dose.

concepts.name: Therapeutic ratio
concepts.statement: Radiotherapy works because cancer cells, reproducing rapidly, are more sensitive to radiation than normal cells. Every technique aims to kill as many abnormal cells as possible for each normal cell killed.

concepts.name: Crossfire beams
concepts.statement: A single beam would give healthy tissue on its path the same dose as the tumor. Rotating the source about a point in the tumor keeps the dose high at the crossing point and spreads it thin everywhere else.

concepts.name: Therapeutic doses
concepts.statement: Doses of tens of sieverts would kill if given to the whole body at once. Localization and fractionation make them survivable, and the tolerable dose depends on the surrounding tissue.

concepts.name: Radiotherapy
concepts.statement: Radiotherapy is the use of ionizing radiation to treat disease, above all to destroy cancer cells.

concepts.name: Food irradiation
concepts.statement: Insects and bacteria are simpler organisms than people and tolerate much more radiation, so killing them takes doses of thousands of grays. A low dose in food irradiation is therefore far larger than a low dose to a person.

concepts.name: No residual radioactivity in irradiated food
concepts.statement: The first worry about irradiated food is that it becomes radioactive. It does not, because $\gamma$ rays, x-rays and electrons at these energies induce no nuclear reactions.

concepts.name: Free radicals and radiolytic products
concepts.statement: Ionizing radiation makes free radicals in food and in organisms, and their reactions produce new compounds called radiolytic products. Free radicals are how irradiation kills organisms, and the radiolytic products are the center of the debate about the safety of irradiated food.

concepts.name: Free radicals
concepts.statement: Free radicals are molecules or atoms with an unpaired electron, made when ionizing radiation breaks molecular bonds; they are highly reactive.

concepts.name: Radiolytic products
concepts.statement: Radiolytic products are the compounds produced in food by the chemical reactions of free radicals that irradiation creates.

concepts.name: Energy from fusion
concepts.statement: The binding energy per nucleon curve of Chapter 31 predicts both fusion and fission. Where two light nuclei make one with greater BE/$A$, mass is destroyed and energy released.

concepts.name: Coulomb barrier
concepts.statement: Two positive nuclei repel each other until they come close enough for the short-ranged nuclear attraction to take over. Their potential energy is therefore a hill, the Coulomb barrier, with a deep well at its center.

concepts.name: Fusion by tunneling
concepts.statement: The core of the Sun is too cool for nuclei to touch, yet it fuses hydrogen. Tunneling explains it, and because tunneling is so sensitive to how high up the barrier the nuclei climb, temperature controls the rate.

concepts.name: Proton-proton cycle
concepts.statement: The Sun shines by the proton-proton cycle, three reactions in which four protons and two electrons become a helium nucleus, two neutrinos and six $\gamma$ rays: $2e^{-} + 4\,{}^{1}\text{H} \to {}^{4}\text{He} + 2v_{\text{e}} + 6\gamma$, releasing 26.7 MeV. The first two reactions must happen twice for each helium nucleus made.

concepts.name: Solar neutrinos
concepts.statement: Energy from the core takes tens of thousands of years to reach the surface, but neutrinos leave in seconds. That makes them the only direct messengers from the reactions, and their shortfall led to the discovery that neutrinos have mass.

concepts.name: Deuterium-tritium fusion
concepts.statement: The proton-proton cycle is far too slow for a power plant. Reactions of deuterium and tritium are easier to induce, give large energies, and use a fuel that is plentiful in sea water.

concepts.name: Finding fusion energy from a mass of fuel
concepts.statement: The energy from fusing a given mass of fuel is the number of reactions in that mass times the energy per reaction, and dividing the energy by the time over which it is released gives the average power.

concepts.name: Break-even and ignition
concepts.statement: Practical fusion needs a hot enough fuel, dense enough, held together long enough; the three trade off against one another. Break-even and ignition are the milestones a reactor must pass.

concepts.name: Magnetic and inertial confinement
concepts.statement: Magnetic confinement holds a hot, thin plasma for a long time in a magnetic field, as in a tokamak, while inertial confinement compresses a dense fuel pellet with laser beams for a very short time. The two techniques trade density against confinement time.

concepts.name: Nuclear fusion
concepts.statement: Nuclear fusion is a reaction in which two nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus.

concepts.name: Break-even
concepts.statement: Break-even is the point at which a fusion reactor produces as much energy from fusion as is put into heating and confining its fuel.

concepts.name: Ignition
concepts.statement: Ignition is the point at which the fusion in a reactor produces enough energy to keep the fuel hot and fusing without any further energy put in.

concepts.name: Magnetic confinement
concepts.statement: Magnetic confinement is the technique of holding a hot fusion plasma away from the walls of its container with magnetic fields, as in a tokamak.

concepts.name: Inertial confinement
concepts.statement: Inertial confinement is the technique of compressing and heating a small pellet of fusion fuel so quickly, usually with laser beams, that it fuses before its own inertia lets it fly apart.

concepts.name: Energy from fission
concepts.statement: Fission is the other side of the binding energy curve. Reading about 7.6 MeV per nucleon near $A = 240$ against 8.6 near $A = 120$ estimates the energy of one fission, about 200 MeV, ten times a fusion and a hundred times a decay.

concepts.name: Calculating fission energy
concepts.statement: The energy released by a fission is the mass destroyed times $c^{2}$, found from the atomic masses of the reactants and of the products, with the neutrons counted among the products.

concepts.name: Neutron-induced fission
concepts.statement: In neutron-induced fission a neutron, having no charge, enters a heavy nucleus at low energy and deposits enough energy to set it oscillating like a struck drop until Coulomb repulsion splits it into two fragments and a few neutrons: $n + {}^{A}\text{X} \to \text{FF}_{1} + \text{FF}_{2} + xn$.

concepts.name: Chain reaction
concepts.statement: Because fission makes neutrons that can cause more fission, a chain reaction is possible when more than one neutron per fission goes on to fission another nucleus. How much material that takes is the critical mass, the central quantity of both reactors and bombs.

concepts.name: Fission of odd-neutron nuclei
concepts.statement: Why ${}^{235}\text{U}$ and ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$ and not the plentiful ${}^{238}\text{U}$? The nuclear force is more attractive when the captured neutron makes the number even, so about 2 MeV more is deposited and the drop deforms further.

concepts.name: Reactor moderation and control
concepts.statement: ${}^{235}\text{U}$ captures slow neutrons best while fission gives fast ones, so a reactor needs a moderator; control rods keep it at criticality. The water also makes a safety feature, since losing it stops the chain reaction.

concepts.name: Finding fission energy from a mass of fuel
concepts.statement: The energy from fissioning a given mass of fuel is the number of nuclei in that mass times the energy per fission. Each fission gives ten times the energy of a fusion, but a kilogram of fission fuel gives only about a quarter as much as a kilogram of fusion fuel, because it holds far fewer nuclei.

concepts.name: Breeding plutonium
concepts.statement: Breeding turns ${}^{238}\text{U}$ into fissile ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$: the ${}^{238}\text{U}$ captures a neutron, and the ${}^{239}\text{U}$ formed decays by two $\beta^{-}$ decays through ${}^{239}\text{Np}$. Breeding makes the other 99 percent of natural uranium usable, and it makes bomb material.

concepts.name: Nuclear fission
concepts.statement: Nuclear fission is a reaction in which a nucleus splits into two or more smaller nuclei.

concepts.name: Fission fragments
concepts.statement: The fission fragments are the two daughter nuclei into which a nucleus splits in fission.

concepts.name: Liquid drop model
concepts.statement: The liquid drop model treats a nucleus as a drop of nuclear matter: energy deposited in it sets it oscillating and deforming, and when it deforms far enough the Coulomb repulsion of its two ends overcomes the short-ranged nuclear attraction and it splits.

concepts.name: Critical mass
concepts.statement: The critical mass is the minimum mass of fissile material needed for a self-sustained chain reaction.

concepts.name: Criticality
concepts.statement: Criticality is the condition in which, on average, exactly one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission, so the chain reaction proceeds at a steady rate.

concepts.name: Supercriticality
concepts.statement: Supercriticality is the condition in which, on average, more than one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission, so the chain reaction grows.

concepts.name: Breeder reactor
concepts.statement: A breeder reactor is a reactor designed to make more fissile fuel, such as ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$ from ${}^{238}\text{U}$, than it consumes.

concepts.name: Fission bomb
concepts.statement: A bomb must hold a supercritical mass together for microseconds before it blows itself apart. The two designs differ in how fast they assemble it, which is why plutonium needed the implosion.

concepts.name: Thermonuclear bomb
concepts.statement: Fusion gives more energy per kilogram, and fast neutrons aid it, so almost nothing limits the size of a fusion bomb. The fission trigger makes tritium and heats the fuel.

concepts.name: Nuclear weapon yield
concepts.statement: The yield of a nuclear weapon is stated in kilotons or megatons of TNT and corresponds to a mass destroyed of a few grams to a few kilograms. Its energy goes into blast, thermal radiation and nuclear radiation in proportions unlike those of a conventional explosive.
